import sys


def reservoir(items, k, draws):
    """Keep k of the items, using the supplied draws instead of a
    random number generator so that the run is reproducible.

    Item i is a candidate for every one of the i + 1 positions seen so
    far, so the draw is reduced modulo i + 1 and not modulo i.
    """
    res = items[:k]
    d = 0
    for i in range(k, len(items)):
        r = draws[d] % (i + 1)
        d += 1
        if r < k:
            res[r] = items[i]
    return res


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    if not data:
        return
    n = int(data[0])
    k = int(data[1])
    items = [int(t) for t in data[2:2 + n]]
    draws = [int(t) for t in data[2 + n:]]

    if k <= 0 or k > n:
        print("bad k")
        return

    res = reservoir(items, k, draws)
    print("kept", " ".join(str(x) for x in res))


main()

explanation:
## The bug

```python
r = draws[d] % i          # wrong
r = draws[d] % (i + 1)    # right
```

The item at index `i` is the `(i + 1)`-th item of the stream. The
algorithm has to choose uniformly among `i + 1` possibilities — the `k`
reservoir slots and the `i + 1 - k` ways of not keeping it — so the
draw is reduced modulo `i + 1`.

Reducing modulo `i` gives a value in `0 .. i - 1`: one possibility
short, every time.

## Working the sample

`n = 6`, `k = 2`, items `10 20 30 40 50 60`, draws `2 0 5 3`. The
reservoir starts as `[10, 20]`.

Correct, with `% (i + 1)`:

| i | item | draw | r | kept? | reservoir |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 30 | 2 | 2 % 3 = 2 | no | `10 20` |
| 3 | 40 | 0 | 0 % 4 = 0 | slot 0 | `40 20` |
| 4 | 50 | 5 | 5 % 5 = 0 | slot 0 | `50 20` |
| 5 | 60 | 3 | 3 % 6 = 3 | no | `50 20` |

Broken, with `% i`:

| i | item | draw | r | kept? | reservoir |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 30 | 2 | 2 % 2 = 0 | slot 0 | `30 20` |
| 3 | 40 | 0 | 0 % 3 = 0 | slot 0 | `40 20` |
| 4 | 50 | 5 | 5 % 4 = 1 | slot 1 | `40 50` |
| 5 | 60 | 3 | 3 % 5 = 3 | no | `40 50` |

Three of the four steps differ. Item 30 is kept when it should not be,
and item 50 goes into the wrong slot.

## What the bias is

With the modulus one short, item `i` is chosen from `i` possibilities
rather than `i + 1`, so it is kept with probability `k / i` instead of
`k / (i + 1)`.

Every item after the first `k` is therefore slightly **too** likely to
survive, and the error grows with position: at `k = 1` and `i = 10` the
item is kept with probability 1/10 instead of 1/11 — a 10% excess — and
at `i = 1000` it is 0.1%. The sample is no longer uniform, and the
early items are the ones that lose out.

It is a bias rather than a crash, it is small for long streams, and no
assertion about the output being a subset of the input would ever catch
it. That is the kind of bug this shape of exercise exists for.

## Why the shape of this exercise matters

A sampler is the classic thing to test badly. "Run it a million times
and check the distribution looks uniform" is a test that fails
occasionally for no reason, takes seconds, and would not have caught a
0.1% bias anyway.

Supplying the draws instead turns a probabilistic algorithm into a
deterministic function. The test is then exact, instant and repeatable,
and it checks the thing that actually matters: that the index
arithmetic is right. The randomness was never the part that was likely
to be wrong.

That separation — the algorithm takes its randomness as a parameter — is
worth doing in real code too. It makes the sampler testable, makes a
run reproducible from a seed, and makes it possible to swap the source
of randomness without touching the algorithm.

## The proof the arithmetic is protecting

By induction: after `m` items, each of them is in the reservoir with
probability `k/m`. When item `m` (0-based, the `(m+1)`-th) arrives it is
kept with probability `k/(m+1)`, which is the base of the step; and an
item already in the reservoir survives with probability

$$1 - \frac{k}{m+1}\cdot\frac{1}{k} = \frac{m}{m+1},$$

so its probability becomes $\frac{k}{m}\cdot\frac{m}{m+1} = \frac{k}{m+1}$.

Both halves of that use `m + 1` in the denominator. Using `m` breaks the
induction immediately, which is the formal version of "the modulus is
one short".
